claims.text: An integrated high-throughput DSC, thermal-expansion, density, and CALPHAD approach can accurately and efficiently determine fusion and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
Arc melting or additive manufacturing can produce homogenized single-phase HEA samples with minimal segregation and uniform microstructure.
Low-temperature heat capacity can be extrapolated toward 0 K using the Debye T^3 law.
The Dulong–Petit limit provides a high-temperature consistency check on measured solid heat capacity.
DSC scans can be extended from cryogenic temperatures to above the melting point under an inert atmosphere and controlled heating rates.
Integrating heat-capacity data over temperature with appropriate extrapolation yields thermal enthalpy and entropy contributions.
The DSC heat-capacity signal rises dramatically when incipient melting begins near the solidus.
The DSC feature near melting can be used to determine the melting temperature.
The DSC signal near melting can be used to determine latent heat or fusion enthalpy.
In-situ thermal-expansion and density measurements can provide the volume change at melting.
CALPHAD modeling can validate and refine experimentally derived fusion quantities in compositionally disordered HEAs.
A uniform single-phase microstructure minimizes processing-induced heterogeneity and makes measured heat capacity and expansion representative of intrinsic configurationally stabilized behavior.
Configurational entropy can make a large contribution to total entropy while alloy-to-alloy differences in thermal entropy are relatively small.
Mixing near equimolar composition increases configurational entropy and, in the ideal-solution limit, lowers liquid Gibbs free energy and melting temperature.
The derived fusion parameters will agree with CALPHAD-predicted trends to within approximately 5–10% across a range of HEA compositions.
Earlier work on equiatomic HEAs such as the Cantor alloy used comparable heat-capacity methods with Debye and Dulong–Petit approximations.
The approach is best suited to single-phase solid-solution HEAs with dominant configurational-entropy contributions.
Multiphase structure, short-range ordering, or segregation can reduce reliability by complicating heat-capacity baselines.
Sample inhomogeneity, overlapping transitions, DSC baseline drift, and deviations in heat capacity near melting are important sources of uncertainty.
Consistent deviations greater than approximately 15% from independent fusion-property measurements and CALPHAD predictions across diverse HEAs would falsify the proposed approach.
